activity.overview: Read a new article on your own and show what you know about main ideas, details, new words and text structure.
activity.passage:
Why Leaves Change Color

In summer, the leaves of most trees are green. The green comes from chlorophyll, a pigment, or coloring, that leaves use to make food from sunlight. A leaf is full of chlorophyll all summer long, and the green hides every other color in the leaf.
In autumn, the days get shorter and the nights get cooler. Trees begin to get ready for winter. They stop making new chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll that is left breaks down. As the green fades, yellow and orange pigments that were in the leaf all along finally show through.
Some trees, such as many maples, also make a new pigment in the fall. It is red or purple. Sunny days and cool nights help trees make more of it, so a fall with bright days and chilly nights often brings the brightest reds.
Finally, a thin layer of cells grows where each leaf joins its twig. It cuts the leaf off from the tree, and the leaf drops. The tree rests through the winter and grows new green leaves in spring.
